CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain the key differences between high-fidelity mockups and functional coded prototypes and when each is appropriate.
Apply transition strategies to convert high-fidelity mockup designs into deployable coded prototypes.
Demonstrate proficiency in using a development environment to build and run a functional prototype.
Design a user proficiency survey that accurately captures participant background and skill level prior to usability testing.
Create a structured usability testing protocol suitable for conducting controlled user studies.
Identify potential risks and failure points in prototype development and testing preparation workflows.

Topics.Title: From Mockup to Functional Prototype
Topics.Summary: Covers the conceptual and practical shift from static high-fidelity mockups to interactive, coded prototypes. Explores what makes a prototype 'functional' and why this transition matters for usability testing.

Elements.Title: Defining Functional Prototypes
Elements.BodyText: A functional prototype is a coded, interactive artifact that simulates real system behavior and can be deployed for user interaction. Unlike a mockup, it responds to user inputs and reflects actual logic flows.
Elements.Notes: Emphasize that functional prototypes are not finished products — they are purpose-built for testing. Students often conflate prototype fidelity with product completeness, which should be addressed explicitly.

Items.Text: Functional prototypes execute real or simulated application logic rather than displaying static screens.
They can be deployed in a controlled environment so that test participants interact with them as they would a real system.
The level of functionality included should be scoped to the specific usability questions being investigated.
Functional prototypes expose timing, responsiveness, and error states that static mockups cannot reveal.

Elements.Title: Limitations of High-Fidelity Mockups for Testing
Elements.BodyText: High-fidelity mockups excel at communicating visual design intent but fall short when realistic interaction data is needed. They cannot capture navigation errors, load behaviors, or user recovery patterns.
Elements.Notes: Students may have invested significant effort in mockups and feel reluctant to move beyond them. Frame this as a natural progression rather than a rejection of prior work.

Items.Text: Mockups require a facilitator to manually advance screens, introducing bias into user interactions.
They cannot surface edge-case behaviors such as empty states, error messages, or multi-step task failures.
Interaction timing and cognitive load data collected from mockups are unreliable for design decisions.

Elements.Title: Criteria for Transition Readiness
Elements.BodyText: Before beginning prototype development, teams should assess whether their mockup designs are stable enough to code against. Premature coding of unstable designs wastes development effort.
Elements.Notes: A useful checkpoint is whether the core user flows have been validated through at least one round of mockup-based feedback. If major structural changes are still expected, delay transition.

Items.Text: Core navigation flows and primary task paths should be finalized in the mockup before coding begins.
Visual design components that will be reused across screens should be identified and documented.
Outstanding design decisions should be logged and resolved or deliberately deferred before development starts.
Team members should agree on a feature scope that is achievable within the available development timeline.

Elements.Title: Scoping the Prototype for Usability Testing
Elements.BodyText: A common mistake is building too much functionality into a test prototype. Scope should be limited to the features and flows directly relevant to the research questions being tested.
Elements.Notes: Use the usability testing protocol as the scoping document — if a feature is not exercised by a test task, it does not need to be functional in the prototype.

Items.Text: Identify the specific tasks participants will perform during testing and build only the flows those tasks require.
Placeholder screens or graceful dead-ends can stand in for out-of-scope functionality.
A narrowly scoped prototype is easier to debug, maintain, and update between test sessions.
Scope decisions should be documented so stakeholders understand what is and is not being tested.

Topics.Title: Transition Strategies from Design to Code
Topics.Summary: Examines practical methods for converting mockup assets and interaction designs into coded prototypes, including handoff practices, component mapping, and iterative build approaches.

Elements.Title: Design Handoff and Asset Preparation
Elements.BodyText: Effective handoff from design to development begins with organizing and exporting mockup assets in formats suitable for coding. Poorly prepared handoffs result in inconsistent implementations.
Elements.Notes: Tools like Figma, Adobe XD, and Sketch provide developer handoff modes that expose spacing, color values, typography, and exportable assets. Encourage students to use these features even if they are both the designer and developer.

Items.Text: Export icons, images, and graphics in appropriate formats and resolutions before coding begins.
Document color tokens, typography scales, and spacing values so they can be implemented consistently in code.
Annotate interaction behaviors — hover states, transitions, and conditional visibility — that are not self-evident from static screens.
Shared component libraries in design tools should map directly to reusable code components where possible.

Elements.Title: Component-First Development Approach
Elements.BodyText: Building reusable interface components before assembling full screens reduces duplication and makes the prototype easier to maintain and update. This mirrors modern front-end development practices.
Elements.Notes: Introduce students to the concept of atomic design if they are unfamiliar — the idea that interfaces are composed of atoms (buttons, inputs), molecules (form groups), and organisms (navigation bars, card lists).

Items.Text: Identify recurring UI patterns in the mockup and build them as standalone, reusable components.
Test each component in isolation before integrating it into full page layouts.
Consistent component naming between design files and code reduces confusion during development.
Reusable components allow rapid iteration when usability testing reveals needed design changes.

Elements.Title: Iterative Build and Continuous Review
Elements.BodyText: Prototype development should proceed in short build cycles, with frequent reviews against the original mockup to catch deviations early. Waiting until the end to compare code output to design leads to costly corrections.
Elements.Notes: Suggest daily or every-other-day comparison passes where the team opens the mockup and the running prototype side by side. Small deviations compound quickly if unchecked.

Items.Text: Build one user flow at a time and review it completely before moving to the next.
Use version control to checkpoint working states so that regressions can be identified and reversed.
Invite a team member who did not build a given flow to review it against the mockup for fresh-eyes feedback.

Elements.Title: Managing Design Drift During Development
Elements.BodyText: Design drift occurs when coding decisions gradually diverge from the approved mockup, producing a prototype that no longer reflects the intended design. Systematic practices prevent unintentional drift.
Elements.Notes: Some drift is deliberate — developers may discover that a designed interaction is technically impractical and need to flag this for a design decision. The goal is not to prevent all deviation but to ensure deviations are conscious and documented.

Items.Text: Establish a clear process for flagging and approving any deviations from the mockup during development.
Document all intentional design changes made during coding so the team retains a change log.
Avoid making ad hoc visual design decisions in code without consulting the design lead.
Regularly test the prototype on the target device type and screen size to catch layout issues early.

Topics.Title: Development Environment Setup and Use
Topics.Summary: Introduces students to the tools and practices needed to establish a functional development environment for building and deploying a testable prototype.

Elements.Title: Choosing an Appropriate Technology Stack
Elements.BodyText: The technology stack for a usability testing prototype should prioritize speed of development and ease of deployment over long-term scalability. The goal is a testable artifact, not a production system.
Elements.Notes: For web-based prototypes, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with a lightweight framework such as React, Vue, or even plain JavaScript are common choices. For native mobile prototypes, consider whether a cross-platform tool like Flutter or React Native meets the need faster than native development.

Items.Text: Select technologies that the team already knows to minimize learning curve during prototype development.
Prioritize stacks that support rapid deployment to a URL or device that test participants can access.
Avoid over-engineering the backend — static sites, mock APIs, or simple JSON data files are sufficient for most usability test prototypes.
The stack choice should support the interaction patterns required by the test tasks.

Elements.Title: Setting Up Version Control
Elements.BodyText: Version control is essential for collaborative prototype development, enabling the team to track changes, revert mistakes, and work in parallel without overwriting each other's contributions.
Elements.Notes: Git with a remote repository on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket is the standard choice. Even solo developers benefit from version control as a safety net during rapid prototype iterations.

Items.Text: Initialize a repository at the start of the project and commit frequently with descriptive messages.
Use branching to develop individual features or flows in isolation before merging into the main prototype.
Establish team conventions for commit messages and branch naming to maintain a readable project history.
Tag release-ready commits so the team can quickly return to a known-good prototype state before each test session.

Elements.Title: Local Development and Live Preview Workflows
Elements.BodyText: A smooth local development workflow allows developers to see the effect of code changes immediately, reducing the iteration cycle between writing code and observing results.
Elements.Notes: Tools like live-server for web projects, or hot-reload features in React and Vue development servers, provide real-time feedback. Mobile emulators and physical device testing should both be part of the local workflow.

Items.Text: Configure a local development server that automatically refreshes the prototype when source files are saved.
Test the prototype on multiple browsers and device types during development, not only at the end.
Use browser developer tools to inspect layout, debug JavaScript, and simulate different screen sizes.
Keep the local environment configuration documented so any team member can set it up from scratch.

Elements.Title: Deploying the Prototype for Testing
Elements.BodyText: Deploying the prototype to an accessible environment before the test session ensures that participants can access it reliably without the need for local setup on their devices.
Elements.Notes: Free hosting options such as GitHub Pages, Netlify, or Vercel work well for web prototypes. For mobile apps, TestFlight (iOS) and internal app sharing via Google Play (Android) are common options. Deployment should be tested at least 24 hours before the first test session.

Items.Text: Deploy to a stable URL or install package well before the testing session to allow time to resolve issues.
Test the deployed prototype on the same device types and network conditions participants will use.
Ensure that any required accounts, login credentials, or test data are configured in the deployed environment.
Have a rollback plan in case the deployed prototype encounters a critical failure during testing.

Topics.Title: Designing User Proficiency Surveys
Topics.Summary: Guides students through the creation of pre-test surveys that assess participant background, technology familiarity, and domain knowledge, enabling more meaningful interpretation of usability test results.

Elements.Title: Purpose and Value of Proficiency Surveys
Elements.BodyText: A user proficiency survey collects structured background information from participants before a usability test, allowing researchers to interpret performance data in light of participant experience levels.
Elements.Notes: Without proficiency data, it is impossible to distinguish whether a usability failure is caused by a design problem or by a mismatch between participant background and target user profile. Proficiency surveys are the foundation of valid participant segmentation.

Items.Text: Proficiency surveys establish whether a participant matches the target user profile for the system being tested.
They allow researchers to analyze whether performance differences correlate with experience levels.
Survey data enables stratified analysis, revealing whether novice and expert users encounter different usability problems.
Collecting this data before the session prevents post-hoc rationalization of anomalous results.

Elements.Title: Identifying Relevant Proficiency Dimensions
Elements.BodyText: Not all background information is relevant to every usability study. Teams must identify the specific dimensions of user experience and knowledge that are most likely to influence performance on the test tasks.
Elements.Notes: Common dimensions include general technology use frequency, familiarity with similar products, domain knowledge, and physical or cognitive accessibility needs. Resist the temptation to ask about everything — longer surveys reduce completion rates and add noise to the data.

Items.Text: Define the user characteristics that are theoretically linked to performance on the specific test tasks.
Consider general digital literacy, domain expertise, and prior use of competing or similar products.
Include demographic items only when they are directly relevant to the research questions.
Limit the survey to items that will actually be used in data analysis to respect participant time.

Elements.Title: Writing Effective Survey Questions
Elements.BodyText: Survey question quality directly affects data reliability. Ambiguous, leading, or double-barreled questions produce unreliable data that cannot support valid conclusions about participant proficiency.
Elements.Notes: Use established question formats: Likert scales for attitude and frequency items, multiple choice for categorical background data, and short open-text fields sparingly. Pre-test the survey with at least two colleagues before deploying it to participants.

Items.Text: Use simple, unambiguous language that participants with varied backgrounds will interpret consistently.
Avoid double-barreled questions that ask about two things simultaneously in a single item.
Provide clearly defined response options that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive.
Pilot-test survey questions with peers to identify confusing wording before participant deployment.

Elements.Title: Structuring and Administering the Survey
Elements.BodyText: The survey should be organized logically, moving from general background questions to more specific proficiency items. Administration timing and format should be designed to minimize burden and maximize completion.
Elements.Notes: Online survey tools such as Google Forms, Qualtrics, or Typeform simplify distribution and response collection. Consider whether the survey will be completed before arrival or at the start of the session, and account for the time required in the session schedule.

Items.Text: Group related questions together and sequence them from general to specific to create a natural flow.
Keep the survey short enough to complete in five to ten minutes without rushing.
Specify whether the survey will be administered online before the session or on-site at the start.
Ensure the survey platform stores responses securely and in a format suitable for analysis.

Topics.Title: Designing Usability Testing Protocols
Topics.Summary: Walks students through creating structured, replicable testing protocols that define participant tasks, facilitator scripts, data collection methods, and session logistics for upcoming user studies.

Elements.Title: Anatomy of a Usability Testing Protocol
Elements.BodyText: A usability testing protocol is a formal document that defines every aspect of how a test session will be conducted, ensuring consistency across participants and enabling replication of the study.
Elements.Notes: The protocol serves as both a planning tool and a session guide. It should be detailed enough that a facilitator who did not design the study could run a session consistently using the document alone.

Items.Text: A complete protocol includes study objectives, participant criteria, task scenarios, facilitator scripts, and data collection procedures.
Standardizing procedures across sessions ensures that differences in participant performance reflect the design, not the session conduct.
The protocol should specify the physical or virtual environment setup required for each session.
All team members should review and sign off on the protocol before testing begins.

Elements.Title: Writing Task Scenarios
Elements.BodyText: Task scenarios describe realistic situations that prompt participants to interact with the prototype in ways that reveal usability strengths and weaknesses. Well-written scenarios feel natural and do not inadvertently guide participants toward correct actions.
Elements.Notes: Avoid using interface terminology in task scenarios — for example, say 'find a way to share this document with a colleague' rather than 'click the Share button.' Scenarios should reflect real contexts of use drawn from user research.

Items.Text: Frame tasks as realistic goals or situations rather than step-by-step instructions.
Do not include interface labels or navigation cues within the task wording.
Each task should correspond to a specific research question or usability hypothesis.
Include both primary tasks and secondary tasks to test core and peripheral functionality.
Define clear completion criteria so facilitators can consistently determine when a task is finished.

Elements.Title: Developing Facilitator Scripts
Elements.BodyText: A facilitator script provides standardized language for introducing the session, delivering tasks, and responding to common participant behaviors such as asking for help or expressing frustration.
Elements.Notes: Scripts prevent facilitator bias by ensuring all participants receive identical instructions. They should include both the spoken text and stage directions for non-verbal cues such as handing over a task card or starting a timer.

Items.Text: Write verbatim introductory text covering the study purpose, consent process, and think-aloud instructions.
Provide scripted neutral responses to common participant requests for help or confirmation.
Include prompts to encourage think-aloud verbalization when participants fall silent.
Script the closing debrief questions to ensure consistent post-task data collection across sessions.

Elements.Title: Planning Data Collection Methods
Elements.BodyText: The protocol must specify what data will be collected, how it will be recorded, and who is responsible for each data collection activity during the session.
Elements.Notes: Common data types include task completion rates, time on task, error counts, think-aloud transcripts, and post-task satisfaction ratings. Screen recording combined with audio capture is the minimum viable setup for remote and in-person sessions.

Items.Text: Define the quantitative metrics to be recorded for each task, such as completion rate and time on task.
Specify qualitative data sources, including think-aloud transcripts, observer notes, and post-task questionnaires.
Assign explicit roles — facilitator, note-taker, and observer — and define what each role records.
Confirm that recording equipment and consent to record are handled before the session begins.

Elements.Title: Session Logistics and Environment Planning
Elements.BodyText: Logistical details such as session scheduling, participant arrival procedures, room or virtual meeting setup, and equipment checks must be planned and documented to prevent disruptions during testing.
Elements.Notes: A pre-session checklist run through 30 minutes before each session can prevent the most common logistical failures. Include items such as prototype deployment status, recording software readiness, and consent form availability.

Items.Text: Schedule sessions with sufficient buffer time between participants to reset the environment and debrief the team.
Document the physical or virtual room setup required, including device placement and screen sharing configuration.
Prepare a pre-session checklist covering equipment, prototype access, and consent documentation.
Conduct at least one full pilot session with a non-participant to test logistics before the first real session.

Elements.Title: Pilot Testing the Protocol
Elements.BodyText: Running a pilot session with a colleague or peer before recruiting actual participants reveals gaps in the protocol, ambiguous task wording, and logistical issues that are not apparent from reading the document alone.
Elements.Notes: Pilot sessions should be treated as seriously as real sessions — use the full script, record the session, and debrief afterward. Treat every problem encountered as a protocol improvement opportunity rather than a personal failure.

Items.Text: Conduct at least one pilot session before the first participant session to validate the protocol end to end.
Use pilot feedback to refine task wording, timing estimates, and facilitator script language.
Verify that all data collection tools and recording systems function correctly during the pilot.
Document changes made after the pilot so the team has a clear record of the final protocol version.

Topics.Title: Integrating Prototype and Testing Preparation
Topics.Summary: Addresses how prototype development and testing protocol design must be coordinated so that the prototype is ready to support exactly the tasks specified in the protocol when testing begins.

Elements.Title: Aligning Prototype Scope with Test Tasks
Elements.BodyText: The prototype must be capable of supporting every task scenario defined in the testing protocol. Misalignment between what the prototype can do and what participants are asked to do invalidates test results.
Elements.Notes: Use the task scenarios as a functional requirements checklist during prototype development. Every task should be walkable end to end in the prototype before the test session is scheduled.

Items.Text: Map each task scenario to the specific prototype flows and features required to complete it.
Conduct an internal walkthrough of every task in the prototype before scheduling participant sessions.
Identify any prototype flows that are incomplete and either fix them or remove the corresponding task from the protocol.
Document the expected completion path for each task so facilitators can recognize correct and incorrect navigation.

Elements.Title: Preparing Test Data and Prototype State
Elements.BodyText: Usability tests require the prototype to begin each session in a consistent, predefined state with appropriate test data pre-loaded so that every participant starts from the same conditions.
Elements.Notes: This is especially important for prototypes that simulate data entry, user accounts, or multi-step workflows. Develop a reset procedure that can be executed quickly between sessions.

Items.Text: Define the initial state of the prototype at the start of each session, including any pre-loaded accounts or content.
Create a reset checklist that restores the prototype to its initial state between participant sessions.
Test the reset procedure during the pilot session to confirm it can be completed within the inter-session buffer time.
Ensure that test data is realistic enough that participants can engage with tasks naturally.

Elements.Title: Coordinating Team Roles Across Development and Testing
Elements.BodyText: The transition from prototype development to test facilitation requires clear role assignments so that team members know their responsibilities during both phases and can support each other effectively.
Elements.Notes: It is common for the developer to serve as technical support during testing rather than as a facilitator, since they can quickly address prototype failures. The person most familiar with the research questions often makes the best facilitator.

Items.Text: Assign a primary facilitator, note-taker, and technical support role before the first session.
Ensure the technical support person knows how to quickly reset or redeploy the prototype if it fails during a session.
Debrief as a team after each session to share observations and adjust the protocol or prototype if needed.
Separate the roles of prototype builder and session facilitator to reduce bias in how tasks are presented.
